title: The pot that stayed cool
told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, a question. has anyone ever changed you without even trying?
options: then you know this story already. listen.

steps.line: On their travels, Mardana once wandered off alone into a deep forest, looking for food.
steps.label: a traditional sakhi

steps.line: There lived Kauda, a fierce man every traveler feared. He caught Mardana, tied him up, and set a huge pot of oil over the fire to throw him in.

steps.q: Mardana is tied up beside a pot of hot oil. Guru Nanak walks into the clearing. What do you think he does?
steps.why: No weapon, no bargain. In the janamsakhis, Guru Nanak often answers cruelty with a song.

steps.line: Guru Nanak came into the clearing and began to sing. Tradition says that however high the fire burned, the oil would not boil. It stayed cool.

steps.q: Why does the story have the oil stay cool?
o: To show the song cooling a burning anger
To prove the Guru had magic powers
steps.why: Guru Nanak refused to do miracles to impress people. Many Sikhs read the cool oil as a picture: the song cooled the fire in Kauda too.

steps.line: Kauda fell at the Guru’s feet and wept. He let Mardana go, and changed his ways. The fiercest man in the forest came out a new one.
Remember the river Bein? Sikhs say Guru Nanak came out of it with a charge: remember the Name, and help others remember. In the forest, that’s what he did.

steps.q: Remembering the Name has a Sikh word: naam simran. What does it look like in everyday life?
o: Reading the Guru’s life once a year
Writing God’s name over the door
Repeating God’s name at work or rest
steps.why: Simran means remembering. Many Sikhs repeat “Waheguru” quietly through the day, while working, walking or falling asleep.

steps.q: Mardana, the friend caught in the forest, was a Muslim musician. What did he play while Guru Nanak sang?
o: The tabla, a pair of drums
steps.why: Bhai Mardana played the rabab through decades of journeys. Sikhs trace their sacred music, kirtan, to this pair: a Muslim player and a Hindu-born Guru.

say: guru nanak never answered cruelty with cruelty. he sang. sikhs believe the name, remembered and sung, can soften even the hardest heart.
the janamsakhis say that in those three days in the river he was taken into god’s presence. everything after, the songs, the long journeys, the hard hearts made soft, is what he came out carrying.

steps.q: Someone has been cruel to a friend of yours. From this story, what would Guru Nanak’s way look like?
o: Go to them, calm and kind, and reach their heart
Shame them in public so they stop
Avoid them and warn everyone else
steps.why: Nanak didn’t ignore the cruelty; he walked straight into the clearing. But he answered it with song, and left room for Kauda to change.

today.say: many sikhs bathe before their dawn prayers, the way guru nanak went to the river each morning. today, when you let water run, at a tap or in the shower, bring to mind a time you went into something hard and came out different. you don’t have to understand it. just say thank you, in whatever way is yours.
options: then let the water carry the thanks.
then i’m with you in the water. you’ll come out.

tomorrow.title: The first words after.
tomorrow.line: four weeks done. next, what guru nanak carried out of the water, and where he took it.

card.keepWhy: A song can cool a burning heart.
sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Kauda (Kauda Rakhshas), the fierce forest man transformed by Guru Nanak after capturing Mardana
Janamsakhi tradition (Puratan) of the Bein river experience at Sultanpur and the charge to remember and share the Name
check: Tellings place Kauda in different regions (central India or Assam) and call him a man-eater; I wrote “a fierce man every traveler feared.”
The oil staying cool is tradition; details vary (in some, the fire would not heat it).

The day-28 topic was the Bein river, already told in week one; this lesson revisits it in one shot and carries “some come back changed” through Kauda. The link (“in the forest, that’s what he did”) is my framing.
